image_provenance.note: The build context is the working tree, so the image carries the checkout's bytes; with core.autocrlf=true those can be CRLF while the blob is LF. Byte equality against the blob and content equality against HEAD are therefore reported separately — a byte mismatch that vanishes under line-ending normalisation is a checkout artifact, not a code difference.

ledger_posture.vacuity_note: An earlier measurement of this step reported the owner UPDATE as 'ok'. It was vacuous: this run's own integration suite had truncated the disposable ledger, so the statement matched zero rows. This run re-arms the suite ledger through append_event before each attempt and records the row count on both sides of it. The incidental emptying is itself a demonstration of the documented TRUNCATE bypass, not a defect in the trigger.
ledger_posture.classification: Two different mechanisms answer, one per identity, and the measurement separates them. The F-05 runtime role is refused by the GRANT layer ('permission denied for table audit_ledger_events') for UPDATE, DELETE and TRUNCATE alike — its statements never reach the trigger. The table owner holds every grant, so only the in-database append-only trigger stands between it and row-level tampering, and that trigger is what refused the owner's UPDATE and DELETE here ('append-only enforcement refuses UPDATE/DELETE on the audit ledger', from audit_ledger_refuse_mutation(), with the sanctioned path named as the poa.ledger_mutation_exception GUC). TRUNCATE bypasses row triggers, so the owner's TRUNCATE of the seeded disposable ledger succeeded (3 rows to 0) while the runtime role was denied it by grants. That is the documented threat-model boundary: an application-level trigger does not defeat a database owner, it defeats the application identity.
